title: allocator-liveness-sweep-experiments-and-small-alloc-bloat
content:
Summary:

This note captures a focused investigation into recurring OOM incidents observed under sustained inference load. The hypothesis we explored: high churn of many small device allocations combined with delayed free semantics (cudaMallocAsync arenas / deferred host frees) produces allocation liveness patterns that cause fragmentation and prevent reuse, ultimately triggering OOM even when aggregate live bytes appear to be well under device capacity.

Context / Why this matters:
- Production inference workload: mixed sequence lengths, many short-lived scratch tensors per request (softmax buffers, rotary cache fragments, intermediate attention outputs).
- We saw intermittent OOMs at tail load (spikes in concurrency + longer sequences). Average memory metrics looked fine; peaks correlated with request concurrency bursts.
- Existing dashboards show high arena high-water marks and steady growth across experiments; free rates are lower than expected after request completion.

What we instrumented:
- Runtime allocator hooks to log: allocation size, stack sample (top 3 frames), arena id (cudaMallocAsync stream allocator), timestamp, request id, and whether allocation returned to pool or was actually released to CUDA.
- Per-request allocation traces (narrow, binary-compressed for retention) and periodic global heap snapshots (sampled every 1s for 300s windows).
- Kernel-level sampling via nvprof/nsys to correlate heavy kernel phases with allocation spikes.
- Synthetic harness that replays live traffic traces (sequence length distribution, token timing, kv cache reuse patterns) at controlled concurrency.

Key observations (empirical):
1) Small-allocation spike behaviour
   - The majority (~62%) of allocations during a request are small buffers between 1KiB and 64KiB (layer norm scratch, fused-op temporaries).
   - These small allocations are often interleaved with a few large KV-cache allocations (multi-MB). Interleaving increases fragmentation because small blocks occupy gaps that would otherwise be coalesced under a simple allocator.

2) Arena growth + delayed purges
   - cudaMallocAsync arms arenas per stream with growth heuristics; we observed arena high-water marks increasing over sequences.
   - Freed memory frequently remained in an arena's free list and was not returned to the OS until an explicit cudaMemPoolTrim or when arena hit a release threshold. Under sustained bursts this means peaks don't allow the arena to shrink between bursts.

3) Liveness skew across requests
   - Some requests hold surprisingly long-lived ephemeral objects due to lazy lifecycle (e.g., tensors held until Python GC of wrapper object) — these show up as top-3 stack samples pointing to higher-level request graph cleanup paths.
   - An anti-pattern: request handlers that queue up finalizers to background threads resulted in delayed device frees by several hundred ms. When concurrency changes rapidly, that delay is enough to cross into OOM territory.

4) Fragmentation amplification from alignment and padding
   - Observed alignment inflation: allocator always aligns to 256B for hotspot paths and 4KiB for certain slabs; many small buffers therefore round up significantly, multiplying effective consumed space of small allocations.

5) Slab/chunk sizing mismatch
   - Our per-size-class slab sizes tuned for CPU allocation characteristics; GPU patterns differ (fewer large allocations but lots of small temporaries). Current slab buckets cause internal fragmentation.

Repro recipe (synthetic):
- Checkout branch: serving-runtime/allocator-instrumentation (see linked PR).
- Run harness: ./tools/replay_trace --trace traces/kv-mixed-1k-20k.json --concurrency 48 --burst-pattern "sine:60s" --enable-alloc-log=stream:0
- Workload config replicates: 30% long sequences (>2048), 50% mid (512–1024), 20% short (<256).
- Repro run that produced OOM for us: concurrency 48, mean inter-token latency tuned to real host (6ms).

Experiments and results:
A) Disable cudaMallocAsync (fallback to cudaMalloc)
   - Result: lower fragmentation in some runs (because cudaMalloc synchronously returned memory and avoided arena growth), but increased per-op latency and host-side stalls. Not acceptable for latency SLOs.

B) Tune arena release threshold (reduce growth factor, trim more aggressively)
   - Lowering growth factor from 1.5x to 1.15x reduced arena high-water by ~18% in steady-state tests. Memory pressure during bursts reduced but alloc/free churn increased (more calls to pool manager). Latency tail increased slightly (~3% tail p99 in microbench).

C) Slab re-sizing and new small-size classes (16B–64KiB)
   - Replacing coarse buckets with finer-grain buckets reduced internal fragmentation for small allocs by ~27%. Combined with reduced alignment to 64B for small paths, peak usage dropped ~12%.

D) Forced synchronous free at request end (explicit cudaStreamSynchronize + release)
   - Solved many OOM repros but caused significant throughput regression. Not viable as default but useful as a debugging mitigation in emergency fallbacks.

E) Bump allocator for ephemeral temporaries (per-request arena)
   - Implemented a per-request bump allocator for very short-lived temporaries (allocated from a pre-reserved device region). At request completion we release the region back to the global pool in O(1).
   - Result: eliminated ~40% of small allocation churn seen in traces; peaks dropped and OOMs resolved in synthetic stress runs. Changes are non-trivial to wire into current core ops but promising.

Root causes (synthesis):
- Combination of many small allocations, coarse alignment, and arena growth heuristics create unusable holes in device memory (fragmentation).
- Deferred frees (background/GC/async stream semantics) mean reuse windows are delayed; when concurrency spikes, many allocs are live simultaneously across age cohorts.
- Mismatch between slab sizing and actual allocation size distribution amplifies internal fragmentation.

Short-term mitigations (low-risk):
- Add telemetry to flag long-lived ephemeral tensors: emit when freed > 100ms after request completion. Start by sampling 1% of requests.
- Reduce default small-allocation alignment from 256B to 64B on hot paths (safe microbench verification required).
- Add a configurable arena trim on low-utilization signals (idle for X seconds) and expose knob to R&D and on-call teams.

Medium-term changes (requires engineering effort):
- Implement per-request bump allocator for ephemeral temporaries; prefer bump for allocations < 64KiB and lifetime within request scope.
- Rework slab class boundaries to match observed distribution and add dynamic rebalancing (periodic histogram-based remap).
- Explore eager coalescing / compaction at safe sync points (e.g., between batches or during warmup windows).

Emergency runbook (for on-call):
1) If OOM spike detected in prod: toggle arena-trim aggressive mode via runtime flag (hot path exposed).
2) Reduce concurrency for affected pool (scale down frontend tokens) to reduce simultaneous live allocations.
3) If memory remains high, enable per-host synchronous release (followed by scheduled rollback) — be aware of latency impact.

Open questions & future experiments:
- Can we safely move more temporaries into host-pinned staging and reuse them without device free pressure? Tradeoffs with host->device transfer cost need quantification.
- Is it possible to implement compacting arenas for GPU (moving live regions)? Likely expensive; investigate feasibility with CUDA peer-copy primitives and model semantics.
- How much of the problem is instrumentation-linked (logging changes temporal behaviour)? Need blind A/B sampling to validate.

Next action items (owners):
- (Maya) Ship small-allocation telemetry flag and 1% sampling pipeline by 2024-10-25.
- (Ethan) Prototype per-request bump allocator RFC and microbench by 2024-11-05.
- (Lina) Run bucket-resizing experiments and provide allocation histograms for last 30 days; propose new boundaries by 2024-10-30.
- (Theo) Add operator-level allocation annotations (mark ephemeral vs persistent) and incremental porting plan; start with LayerNorm and attention softmax ops.

Appendix: quick logs excerpt (sanitized)
- sample allocation stream (times in ms):
  [t=10124] alloc 48KiB stream0 stack: attention_forward:softmax -> fused_op_tmp -> request_handler
  [t=10124] alloc 3.2MiB stream0 stack: kv_cache_alloc -> cache_manager -> request_handler
  [t=10124] free 48KiB  (queued, not returned to pool)
  [t=10124] alloc 56KiB stream1 ...
  [t=10125] arena[0] highwater 5.4GiB
  [t=10126] OOM at alloc 1.8MiB -> cannot satisfy from any free region (fragmentation)

Notes on reproducibility: keep replayed inter-token timing realistic; synthetic fast-fire workloads change allocator behaviour (they look worse but not representative). Aim for a bursty-but-real pattern.

End.
